terms.plain: rising prices
terms.meaning: Prices of most things going up over time, so each dollar buys a little less than it used to.
terms.example: A coffee that cost $3 last year costs $3.20 this year.

terms.plain: falling prices
terms.meaning: Prices of most things going down over time. Sounds nice, but people delay buying and businesses earn less.
terms.example: A TV that cost $500 last year costs $450 now, so you wait to see if it drops more.

terms.plain: prices rising more slowly
terms.meaning: Prices are still going up, just not as fast as before.
terms.example: Prices rose 8% last year but only 3% this year.

terms.plain: stalled growth with rising prices
terms.meaning: The worst of both worlds: prices keep going up while jobs and growth are stuck.
terms.example: Groceries get pricier every month while your employer freezes hiring.

terms.plain: runaway rising prices
terms.meaning: Prices rising so fast that money loses value week to week or even day to day.
terms.example: A loaf of bread costs twice as much on Friday as it did on Monday.

terms.plain: the everyday-prices index
terms.meaning: A monthly measure of what a typical basket of household goods and services costs. It is the usual way inflation is tracked.
terms.example: If the index rises 3%, the same groceries, rent, and gas cost about 3% more than a year ago.

terms.plain: rising prices excluding food and energy
terms.meaning: Inflation measured without food and fuel, because those prices swing around a lot and can hide the underlying trend.
terms.example: Gas spiked this month, but core inflation shows most other prices barely moved.

terms.plain: what everyday life costs
terms.meaning: How much money it takes to cover basics like housing, food, and transport in a given place.
terms.example: The same salary stretches further in a small town than in a big city.

terms.plain: how much your money actually buys
terms.meaning: The real value of money measured by what it can buy, not the number printed on it.
terms.example: $100 bought a full cart of groceries in 2010 and about half a cart now.

terms.plain: after adjusting for rising prices
terms.meaning: A number that has been corrected for inflation so you can compare different years fairly.
terms.example: A 5% raise when prices rose 6% is a pay cut in real terms.

terms.plain: before adjusting for rising prices
terms.meaning: The raw dollar number, not corrected for inflation.
terms.example: Your nominal pay went from $50k to $52k, but if prices rose 5%, you can actually buy less.

terms.plain: the general level of prices
terms.meaning: The average of all prices in the economy at a point in time.
terms.example: When the price level rises, nearly everything, from rent to haircuts, costs more.

terms.plain: a legal maximum price
terms.meaning: A cap set by the government on how much something can be sold for.
terms.example: Rent control that stops a landlord from charging more than $1,500 a month.

terms.plain: a legal minimum price
terms.meaning: A bottom limit set by the government on how cheaply something can be sold.
terms.example: The minimum wage is a price floor on what an hour of work can be paid.

terms.plain: prices that are slow to change
terms.meaning: Prices and wages that do not adjust quickly even when conditions change.
terms.example: A restaurant keeps its menu prices the same for a year because reprinting menus is a hassle.

terms.plain: the total value of everything a country produces
terms.meaning: The total value of all goods and services made in a country in a year. It is the standard scorecard for the size of an economy.
terms.example: Every car built, haircut given, and app sold in the US in a year, added up into one number.

terms.plain: output per person
terms.meaning: The country's total output divided by its population. A rough guide to average living standards.
terms.example: Two countries can have the same GDP, but the one with fewer people is richer per person.

terms.plain: the economy getting bigger
terms.meaning: The economy producing more stuff than it did before, usually measured as a percentage change per year.
terms.example: The economy grew 2%, meaning the country made about 2% more goods and services than last year.

terms.plain: a shrinking economy
terms.meaning: A period, usually a few months or more, when the economy shrinks: less is produced, businesses cut back, and people lose jobs.
terms.example: Stores close, hiring stops, and your neighbors get laid off.

terms.plain: a deep, long-lasting shrinking economy
terms.meaning: A very severe recession that lasts years rather than months.
terms.example: The 1930s, when a quarter of workers had no job.

terms.plain: bounce-back
terms.meaning: The period after a recession when output and jobs start growing again.
terms.example: Restaurants reopen and start hiring again after a bad year.

terms.plain: growth period
terms.meaning: A stretch of time when the economy is getting bigger.
terms.example: Years when businesses keep opening and unemployment keeps falling.

terms.plain: the economy's ups and downs
terms.meaning: The natural pattern of the economy growing, then shrinking, then growing again over several years.
terms.example: Boom years followed by a slump followed by another boom.

terms.plain: slowing the economy without a crash
terms.meaning: When a central bank cools down an overheated economy just enough to tame inflation without causing a recession.
terms.example: Braking gently to slow a car rather than slamming the brakes.

terms.plain: slowing the economy so much it crashes
terms.meaning: When efforts to cool inflation push the economy into a recession.
terms.example: Hitting the brakes so hard the car skids.

terms.plain: output per hour of work
terms.meaning: How much gets made for each hour worked. Higher productivity means more stuff from the same effort.
terms.example: A worker with a power drill builds more furniture per day than one with a screwdriver.

terms.plain: production
terms.meaning: The total goods and services made.
terms.example: A factory's output is the number of cars it builds.

terms.plain: the gap between what the economy makes and what it could make
terms.meaning: The difference between actual production and what the economy could produce if everyone and everything were fully used.
terms.example: A factory running at 70% capacity has a 30% gap.

terms.plain: what the economy could make at full stretch
terms.meaning: The most the economy could produce without pushing prices up too fast.
terms.example: The top speed a car can safely go for a long trip.

terms.plain: total spending in the economy
terms.meaning: All the spending by households, businesses, government, and foreigners on a country's goods and services, added together.
terms.example: Everyone's shopping, every company's investment, and government projects, all combined.

terms.plain: total production in the economy
terms.meaning: Everything businesses in a country are willing and able to make at a given price level.
terms.example: All the factories, farms, and shops together deciding how much to produce.

terms.plain: household spending
terms.meaning: Money that people spend on goods and services for themselves.
terms.example: Groceries, rent, Netflix, and new shoes.

terms.plain: spending on buildings and machines
terms.meaning: In economics, money spent on buildings, machines, and tools that help make more things later. Not the same as buying stocks.
terms.example: A bakery buying a new oven.

terms.plain: tools, buildings, and machines
terms.meaning: The physical stuff, and sometimes the money, a business uses to produce goods and services.
terms.example: A carpenter's workshop and tools.

terms.plain: people's skills and knowledge
terms.meaning: The education, training, and experience that make workers more valuable.
terms.example: A nurse's years of training.

terms.plain: workers
terms.meaning: The people and the work they do to produce things.
terms.example: Every employee from cashier to CEO.

terms.plain: the basic ingredients for making things
terms.meaning: Land, workers, tools, and know-how: the inputs every business needs.
terms.example: For a farm: the field, the farmers, the tractor, and the owner's judgment.

terms.plain: the number of people who can't find work
terms.meaning: The share of people who are looking for work but do not have a job.
terms.example: Out of 100 people who want a job, 5 cannot find one, so unemployment is 5%.

terms.plain: nearly everyone who wants a job has one
terms.meaning: The point where unemployment is as low as it can realistically go, with only people between jobs still looking.
terms.example: Every restaurant in town has a 'now hiring' sign.

terms.plain: having less work than you want
terms.meaning: Working part time when you want full time, or in a job below your skill level.
terms.example: An engineer driving a taxi while looking for engineering work.

terms.plain: joblessness because skills no longer match the jobs
terms.meaning: People out of work because the jobs they know how to do have disappeared or moved.
terms.example: Coal miners in a town where the mine closed.

terms.plain: joblessness caused by a weak economy
terms.meaning: People losing jobs because the economy is in a slump, not because of their skills.
terms.example: A construction worker laid off during a housing bust.

terms.plain: joblessness from being between jobs
terms.meaning: Short spells of unemployment as people move between jobs or enter the workforce.
terms.example: A new graduate spending two months job hunting.

terms.plain: the share of adults working or looking for work
terms.meaning: The percentage of working-age people who either have a job or are actively looking for one.
terms.example: Retirees and stay-at-home parents are not counted as participating.

terms.plain: the monthly jobs count
terms.meaning: The US government's monthly count of how many jobs were added or lost, excluding farm work.
terms.example: Headlines like 'the economy added 200,000 jobs last month'.

terms.plain: the lowest legal pay
terms.meaning: The least an employer is legally allowed to pay per hour.
terms.example: A cashier must be paid at least $15 an hour in some states.

terms.plain: pay rising
terms.meaning: How fast workers' pay is going up over time.
terms.example: Average hourly pay rose 4% over the year.

terms.plain: pay after adjusting for rising prices
terms.meaning: What your paycheck can actually buy, once inflation is accounted for.
terms.example: A 3% raise when prices rose 3% means your real wage did not change.

terms.plain: take-home pay
terms.meaning: The money you have left after taxes to spend or save.
terms.example: Your paycheck after taxes come out.

terms.plain: spending money
terms.meaning: What is left after taxes and essentials like rent and food.
terms.example: The money you can spend on a concert or a vacation.

terms.plain: the central bank's control of interest rates and money
terms.meaning: The tools a central bank uses, mainly interest rates, to keep prices stable and the economy steady.
terms.example: The Fed raising rates to cool inflation.

terms.plain: the government's taxing and spending
terms.meaning: How the government uses taxes and spending to influence the economy.
terms.example: Sending stimulus checks or cutting taxes during a slump.

terms.plain: the country's main bank
terms.meaning: The institution that controls a country's money supply and interest rates.
terms.example: The Federal Reserve in the US or the Bank of England in the UK.

terms.plain: the Fed
terms.meaning: America's central bank. It sets the key interest rate, and its decisions ripple out to mortgages, car loans, and credit cards.
terms.example: When the news says 'the Fed raised rates', your credit card interest will probably go up too.

terms.plain: the cost of borrowing money
terms.meaning: The percentage you pay to borrow money, or earn for lending it.
terms.example: Borrow $1,000 at 5% and you owe $50 extra a year.

terms.plain: the Fed's key interest rate
terms.meaning: The rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, set by the Federal Reserve. Most other interest rates follow it.
terms.example: When this goes up, mortgage and credit card rates soon go up too.

terms.plain: an interest rate increase
terms.meaning: The central bank raising its main interest rate to make borrowing more expensive.
terms.example: After a rate hike, a new car loan costs more per month.

terms.plain: an interest rate decrease
terms.meaning: The central bank lowering its main interest rate to make borrowing cheaper.
terms.example: After a rate cut, mortgages get cheaper and more people buy homes.

terms.plain: the central bank creating money to buy bonds
terms.meaning: A central bank buying large amounts of bonds with newly created money to push interest rates down and encourage lending.
terms.example: Like the Fed flooding the system with cash to keep borrowing cheap.

terms.plain: the central bank shrinking the money it created
terms.meaning: The reverse of quantitative easing: the central bank lets its bond holdings shrink, pulling money out of the system.
terms.example: The Fed slowly draining the extra cash it pumped in earlier.

terms.plain: the total amount of money in the economy
terms.meaning: All the cash and bank deposits available in the economy.
terms.example: Every dollar in wallets and checking accounts added together.

terms.plain: how easily something turns into cash
terms.meaning: How quickly and cheaply you can convert something into spendable money. Also used for how much ready cash is sloshing around.
terms.example: Cash is very liquid; a house is not, because selling it takes months.

terms.plain: hard to turn into cash
terms.meaning: Something that cannot be sold quickly without losing value.
terms.example: A rare painting or a house.

terms.plain: the cash banks must keep on hand
terms.meaning: The minimum share of deposits a bank must hold rather than lend out.
terms.example: If you deposit $100 and the requirement is 10%, the bank keeps $10 and can lend $90.

terms.plain: banks lending out most of what you deposit
terms.meaning: The system where banks keep only a fraction of deposits in reserve and lend the rest.
terms.example: Your $1,000 deposit becomes someone else's $900 car loan.

terms.plain: everyone rushing to pull their money out of a bank
terms.meaning: When many customers withdraw at once because they fear the bank will fail, which can actually cause it to fail.
terms.example: Lines around the block at a bank in 1930, or a viral tweet emptying accounts overnight.

terms.plain: the emergency lender to banks
terms.meaning: A central bank's role of lending to banks that cannot borrow anywhere else, to stop a panic.
terms.example: The Fed lending to a bank so it can pay depositors during a scare.

terms.plain: borrowed money
terms.meaning: Money lent to a person or business that must be paid back, usually with interest.
terms.example: A credit card, a mortgage, or a business loan.

terms.plain: a sudden shortage of loans
terms.meaning: When banks abruptly stop lending or make loans much harder to get.
terms.example: Businesses with good records suddenly cannot get a loan to make payroll.

terms.plain: borrowed money
terms.meaning: Using debt to make a bigger bet or purchase than you could with your own money alone. It magnifies both gains and losses.
terms.example: Buying a $500k house with $50k down: a 10% price rise doubles your money, a 10% fall wipes it out.

terms.plain: debt-funded
terms.meaning: Done with a lot of borrowed money, which magnifies both gains and losses.
terms.example: A leveraged buyout is a company purchase paid for mostly with loans.

terms.plain: paying down debt
terms.meaning: Reducing how much borrowed money is being used.
terms.example: A family cutting spending to pay off credit cards.

terms.plain: being able to pay all your debts
terms.meaning: Having more assets than debts, so you could pay everything you owe if you had to.
terms.example: A business that owns $1M of stuff and owes $600k is solvent.

terms.plain: owing more than you have
terms.meaning: When debts exceed assets and bills cannot be paid.
terms.example: A company that owes $1M but only has $600k in total.

terms.plain: failing to pay back a loan
terms.meaning: Not making the required payments on a debt.
terms.example: Missing your mortgage payments for months.

terms.plain: taking risks because someone else will cover the losses
terms.meaning: When people behave more recklessly because they know they will be protected from the consequences.
terms.example: Driving less carefully because you have full insurance.

terms.plain: a rescue with public money
terms.meaning: The government stepping in with money to save a failing company or bank.
terms.example: Taxpayers propping up a bank so it does not collapse.

terms.plain: the government spending more than it collects
terms.meaning: When the government spends more in a year than it takes in through taxes, and borrows to cover the difference.
terms.example: Earning $50k but spending $55k, and putting the extra on a credit card.
terms.plural: years of the government spending more than it collects

terms.plain: the government collecting more than it spends
terms.meaning: When the government takes in more tax than it spends in a year.
terms.example: Earning $50k and spending only $45k.

terms.plain: everything the government owes
terms.meaning: The total amount the government has borrowed over the years and not yet paid back.
terms.example: The country's running credit card balance.

terms.plain: government debt compared to the size of the economy
terms.meaning: How big the national debt is relative to what the country produces in a year. A way to judge whether debt is manageable.
terms.example: Owing $100k on a $100k salary versus a $30k salary.

terms.plain: government spending cuts and tax hikes
terms.meaning: Policies that cut public spending or raise taxes to reduce government borrowing.
terms.example: Closing libraries and raising sales tax to balance the budget.

terms.plain: government spending to boost the economy
terms.meaning: Extra government spending or tax cuts meant to get a weak economy moving.
terms.example: Stimulus checks mailed to households during a downturn.

terms.plain: government money that lowers a price
terms.meaning: A payment from the government to make something cheaper to produce or buy.
terms.example: Tax credits that knock $7,500 off an electric car.

terms.plain: a tax on imports
terms.meaning: A tax charged on goods brought in from another country, which makes them more expensive.
terms.example: A 25% tariff on foreign steel makes imported steel cost 25% more.

terms.plain: a tax that takes a bigger share from higher earners
terms.meaning: A tax where the rate goes up as income goes up.
terms.example: Someone earning $500k pays a higher percentage than someone earning $40k.

terms.plain: a tax that hits lower earners harder
terms.meaning: A tax that takes a bigger share of income from people who earn less.
terms.example: Sales tax: a $10 tax is a bigger chunk of a $300 weekly paycheck than a $3,000 one.

terms.plain: the tax on your next dollar
terms.meaning: The rate you pay on the last, or next, dollar you earn, not on all your income.
terms.example: Being in the 24% bracket does not mean 24% of everything; only income above a threshold is taxed at 24%.

terms.plain: government money given to people
terms.meaning: Payments from the government to individuals without anything in return, like benefits.
terms.example: Social Security, unemployment benefits, food stamps.

terms.plain: government benefit programs people qualify for by law
terms.meaning: Programs that pay benefits to anyone who meets the rules.
terms.example: Social Security and Medicare.

terms.plain: built-in cushions in the budget
terms.meaning: Parts of the tax and benefit system that automatically soften a downturn without new laws.
terms.example: When people lose jobs, unemployment benefits kick in and their tax bills fall.

terms.plain: government borrowing squeezing out private borrowing
terms.meaning: When heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates and makes it harder for businesses to borrow.
terms.example: A big government bond sale soaks up money that would have funded a startup.

terms.plain: things everyone can use and no one can be excluded from
terms.meaning: Goods like streetlights or national defense that benefit everyone and cannot easily be sold person by person.
terms.example: A lighthouse helps every ship, whether or not they paid for it.

terms.plain: a side effect on people not involved
terms.meaning: A cost or benefit that lands on someone who was not part of the deal.
terms.example: A factory's pollution making a neighbor sick, or a neighbor's garden making your street nicer.
terms.plural: side effects on people not involved

terms.plain: the market getting it wrong on its own
terms.meaning: A situation where buying and selling freely leads to a bad outcome for society, so rules may be needed.
terms.example: Nobody pays for clean air, so factories pollute too much.

terms.plain: government rules for businesses
terms.meaning: Laws that limit or direct what businesses can do.
terms.example: Food safety inspections and limits on bank risk-taking.

terms.plain: removing government rules
terms.meaning: Loosening or scrapping rules on businesses.
terms.example: Letting airlines set their own fares and routes.

terms.plain: the government taking over a business
terms.meaning: The government taking ownership of a company or industry.
terms.example: The state taking over a failing railroad.

terms.plain: selling a government business to private owners
terms.meaning: Transferring a state-owned company or service into private hands.
terms.example: A city selling its water utility to a company.

terms.plain: how much is available versus how much people want
terms.meaning: The two forces that set prices: how much sellers offer and how much buyers want. Scarce and popular things cost more.
terms.example: Concert tickets cost more when there are few seats and many fans.

terms.plain: how much is available to sell
terms.meaning: The amount of something that sellers are willing to offer at a given price.
terms.example: Farmers bring more tomatoes to market when tomato prices are high.

terms.plain: how much people want to buy
terms.meaning: The amount of something that buyers want and can pay for at a given price.
terms.example: More people want ice cream on a hot day.

terms.plain: the balance point where supply matches demand
terms.meaning: The price where the amount people want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.
terms.example: The ticket price where the venue sells out exactly, with no empty seats and no one turned away.

terms.plain: not enough to go around
terms.meaning: When people want to buy more of something than is available at the current price.
terms.example: Empty shelves where the toilet paper used to be.

terms.plain: too much to sell
terms.meaning: When there is more of something than people want to buy at the current price.
terms.example: A warehouse full of unsold TVs after the holidays.

terms.plain: how much buying changes when the price changes
terms.meaning: A measure of how sensitive people are to price. Elastic means a small price change causes a big change in buying. Inelastic means people keep buying regardless.
terms.example: Raise the price of one brand of soda and people switch (elastic). Raise the price of insulin and people still buy (inelastic).

terms.plain: price-sensitive
terms.meaning: Describes something people buy a lot less of when its price rises, usually because there are easy alternatives.
terms.example: Raise the price of one brand of soda and people just switch brands.

terms.plain: not price-sensitive
terms.meaning: Describes something people keep buying about the same amount of even when the price rises, because they need it or have no alternative.
terms.example: Raise the price of insulin or gas and people still buy nearly as much.

terms.plain: what you give up by choosing one thing over another
terms.meaning: The value of the next best option you did not take.
terms.example: Spending Saturday at work means giving up the day at the beach.

terms.plain: not enough for everyone who wants it
terms.meaning: The basic problem that wants are unlimited but resources are not.
terms.example: There is only so much land, time, and money to go around.

terms.plain: the effect of one more
terms.meaning: Relating to a small additional amount: the extra cost or benefit of one more unit.
terms.example: The marginal cost of one more pizza is just the extra dough and cheese.

terms.plain: each extra bit helps less than the last
terms.meaning: The point where adding more of something gives smaller and smaller gains.
terms.example: The first slice of pizza is great; the fifth, not so much.

terms.plain: getting cheaper per unit as you make more
terms.meaning: Big producers can make each item more cheaply because fixed costs get spread over more units.
terms.example: A bakery making 1,000 loaves pays less per loaf than one making 10.

terms.plain: being relatively better at one thing
terms.meaning: The idea that everyone gains when each person or country focuses on what they do best relative to other tasks, then trades.
terms.example: A lawyer who types fast still hires a typist, because the lawyer's time is worth more in court.

terms.plain: an edge over rivals
terms.meaning: Something that lets a business beat its competitors, like lower costs or a better product.
terms.example: A cafe on the only corner with parking.

terms.plain: one seller controlling the market
terms.meaning: A market with a single seller and no real competition, which usually means higher prices.
terms.example: The only internet provider in town.
terms.plural: markets controlled by a single seller

terms.plain: a few big sellers controlling the market
terms.meaning: A market dominated by a handful of large companies.
terms.example: The few big airlines or phone carriers.

terms.plain: one buyer controlling the market
terms.meaning: A market with a single dominant buyer, which can push prices or wages down.
terms.example: A town where one factory is the only employer.

terms.plain: rivals secretly agreeing to fix prices
terms.meaning: A group of competitors who agree to limit supply or set prices instead of competing.
terms.example: OPEC countries agreeing to pump less oil to keep prices high.

terms.plain: many small sellers with identical products
terms.meaning: A textbook market where no single seller can influence the price.
terms.example: Hundreds of farmers all selling the same wheat.

terms.plain: obstacles that keep new competitors out
terms.meaning: Things that make it hard for a new business to enter a market.
terms.example: The huge cost of building a chip factory.

terms.plain: laws against unfair market dominance
terms.meaning: Rules that stop companies from crushing competition or fixing prices.
terms.example: Regulators blocking a merger that would leave one grocery chain in a region.

terms.plain: buying and selling without government interference
terms.meaning: An economy where prices are set by buyers and sellers, not by the government.
terms.example: A farmers' market where each stall sets its own prices.

terms.plain: self-interest accidentally helping everyone
terms.meaning: Adam Smith's idea that people pursuing their own gain in a market end up benefiting society.
terms.example: The baker bakes bread to make money, and you get to eat.

terms.plain: profiting by gaming the rules rather than creating value
terms.meaning: Trying to get richer by lobbying, monopoly, or special treatment instead of making something useful.
terms.example: A company lobbying for a rule that bans its competitors.

terms.plain: extra profit beyond what is needed
terms.meaning: Payment above what would be necessary to keep a resource in use, often from owning something scarce.
terms.example: A landlord charging far more simply because the location is unique.

terms.plain: buying cheap in one place and selling dear in another
terms.meaning: Profiting from a price difference for the same thing in two markets.
terms.example: Buying a sneaker for $100 at one store and selling it for $150 online.

terms.plain: betting on price moves
terms.meaning: Buying something not to use it but hoping to sell it later for more.
terms.example: Buying a condo to flip, not to live in.

terms.plain: prices soaring far above what something is worth
terms.meaning: When prices rise way beyond any sensible value because everyone expects them to keep rising, until they crash.
terms.example: Tulip bulbs selling for the price of a house in 1637.
terms.plural: prices soaring far above what things are worth

terms.plain: a basic raw good
terms.meaning: A standard product that is the same no matter who makes it, like oil or wheat.
terms.example: A barrel of oil is a barrel of oil, whoever pumped it.

terms.plain: a shopper
terms.meaning: Anyone who buys goods or services for their own use.
terms.example: You, at the grocery store.

terms.plain: a family
terms.meaning: Economists' word for the people who live together and share money: a family, a couple, or one person living alone.
terms.example: Two roommates splitting rent count as one household.

terms.plain: a business that makes things
terms.meaning: Anyone who creates goods or services to sell.
terms.example: A farmer, a factory, or a freelance designer.

terms.plain: things you can buy
terms.meaning: Goods are physical things; services are work done for you.
terms.example: A phone is a good; a haircut is a service.

terms.plain: satisfaction
terms.meaning: The economist's word for the benefit or happiness you get from something.
terms.example: The enjoyment of a good meal.

terms.plain: overall well-being
terms.meaning: In economics, how well off people are in total, not just the benefit program.
terms.example: Whether a policy leaves people better or worse off overall.

terms.plain: a reason to act a certain way
terms.meaning: Something that motivates a person or business to make a choice.
terms.example: A bonus for hitting a sales target.
terms.plural: reasons to act a certain way

terms.plain: someone who weighs costs and benefits
terms.meaning: The textbook assumption that people make decisions to get the most benefit for themselves.
terms.example: Choosing the cheaper of two identical products.

terms.plain: how people really decide, quirks and all
terms.meaning: The study of how real people make economic choices, including habits, biases, and mistakes.
terms.example: People buying more when a price ends in .99.

terms.plain: one person's gain is another's loss
terms.meaning: A situation where the total is fixed, so whatever one side wins the other loses.
terms.example: Splitting a single pie.

terms.plain: everyone overusing a shared resource
terms.meaning: When individuals each take a bit more of a shared resource, it gets used up for everyone.
terms.example: Overfishing a lake until there are no fish left.

terms.plain: one side knowing more than the other
terms.meaning: When one party in a deal has information the other lacks.
terms.example: A used-car seller knowing the car has problems the buyer cannot see.

terms.plain: the wrong customers signing up
terms.meaning: When the people most likely to cost you are the ones most eager to buy.
terms.example: Only sick people buying health insurance, driving premiums up.

terms.plain: the gap from buying more abroad than we sell
terms.meaning: When a country imports more than it exports.
terms.example: The US buying $100 of goods from abroad while selling $70 to other countries.

terms.plain: the surplus from selling more abroad than we buy
terms.meaning: When a country exports more than it imports.
terms.example: Germany selling more cars abroad than it buys in foreign goods.

terms.plain: the gap between exports and imports
terms.meaning: The difference between what a country sells abroad and what it buys from abroad.
terms.example: Sell $80 abroad, buy $100 from abroad: a $20 shortfall.

terms.plain: goods sold to other countries
terms.meaning: Things made at home and sold abroad.
terms.example: American soybeans shipped to China.

terms.plain: goods bought from other countries
terms.meaning: Things made abroad and bought at home.
terms.example: A phone assembled in Vietnam sold in Ohio.

terms.plain: shielding local businesses from foreign competition
terms.meaning: Using tariffs, quotas, or rules to make imports harder so local companies face less competition.
terms.example: Taxing foreign cars so people buy domestic ones.

terms.plain: buying and selling across borders without barriers
terms.meaning: Trade between countries without tariffs or quotas.
terms.example: Goods flowing between US states without any border tax.

terms.plain: a limit on how much can be imported
terms.meaning: A cap on the quantity of a product allowed into a country.
terms.example: Only 1 million foreign cars allowed in per year.
terms.plural: limits on how much can be imported

terms.plain: what one currency is worth in another
terms.meaning: The price of one country's money in terms of another's.
terms.example: One dollar buys 0.90 euros today.

terms.plain: making a currency worth less on purpose
terms.meaning: A government deliberately lowering the value of its currency against others.
terms.example: China letting the yuan weaken so its exports get cheaper.

terms.plain: losing value over time
terms.meaning: A currency or asset becoming worth less. For currencies, it means one unit buys less foreign money.
terms.example: The pound falling from $1.40 to $1.20, or a car losing value each year.

terms.plain: gaining value over time
terms.meaning: A currency or asset becoming worth more.
terms.example: The dollar rising so your vacation in Europe gets cheaper.

terms.plain: a dollar that buys a lot of foreign currency
terms.meaning: When the dollar is worth more against other currencies, making imports and foreign travel cheaper but exports harder to sell.
terms.example: Your trip to Paris costs less, but US farmers sell less abroad.

terms.plain: a dollar that buys less foreign currency
terms.meaning: When the dollar is worth less against other currencies, making imports pricier but exports easier to sell.
terms.example: Foreign goods cost more, but foreign buyers snap up US products.

terms.plain: countries becoming more economically connected
terms.meaning: The growing flow of goods, money, people, and ideas across borders.
terms.example: A phone designed in California, built in China, sold in Brazil.

terms.plain: moving work to another country
terms.meaning: Relocating production or jobs abroad, usually to cut costs.
terms.example: A call center moving from Ohio to the Philippines.

terms.plain: fast-growing poorer countries
terms.meaning: Developing countries whose economies are growing quickly but are still catching up.
terms.example: India, Brazil, Indonesia.

terms.plain: penalties on a country's trade or finances
terms.meaning: Restrictions one country places on another's trade or banking to punish or pressure it.
terms.example: Banning imports of Russian oil.

terms.plain: foreign companies building or buying businesses here
terms.meaning: Money from abroad used to start or buy businesses in a country.
terms.example: A Japanese carmaker building a plant in Tennessee.

terms.plain: money rushing out of a country
terms.meaning: Investors quickly moving their money abroad, usually out of fear.
terms.example: Wealthy people wiring savings overseas when a crisis hits.

terms.plain: the chain of steps that gets a product to you
terms.meaning: All the companies and steps involved in making and delivering a product.
terms.example: Cotton farm to fabric mill to factory to store to your closet.
terms.plural: the chains of steps that get products to you

terms.plain: an IOU that pays interest
terms.meaning: A loan you make to a government or company. They pay you interest and return the money at a set date.
terms.example: Lend the government $1,000 for 10 years and collect $40 a year.

terms.plain: the interest return
terms.meaning: The yearly income from a bond or investment as a percentage of its price.
terms.example: A $1,000 bond paying $50 a year has a 5% yield.

terms.plain: the line of interest rates from short to long loans
terms.meaning: A chart showing interest rates for loans of different lengths. Normally longer loans pay more.
terms.example: A 1-year bond at 4% and a 10-year bond at 5% make an upward-sloping curve.

terms.plain: short-term loans paying more than long-term ones
terms.meaning: When short-term interest rates are higher than long-term ones, an unusual situation that often comes before a recession.
terms.example: A 2-year bond paying more than a 10-year bond.

terms.plain: ownership in a company
terms.meaning: A share of ownership, or the value of what you own minus what you owe on it.
terms.example: Owning shares in Apple, or the part of your house you have actually paid off.

terms.plain: a company's cash payout to shareholders
terms.meaning: A slice of profits a company pays to the people who own its shares.
terms.example: Getting $2 per share every quarter.
terms.plural: cash payouts to a company's owners

terms.plain: something you own that has value
terms.meaning: Anything of value that can be owned, like cash, a house, or shares.
terms.example: Your car, savings account, and retirement fund.
terms.plural: things you own that have value

terms.plain: something you owe
terms.meaning: A debt or obligation to pay.
terms.example: Your mortgage and credit card balance.

terms.plain: the collection of investments someone owns
terms.meaning: All of an investor's holdings, taken together.
terms.example: Your mix of stocks, bonds, and savings.

terms.plain: not putting all your eggs in one basket
terms.meaning: Spreading investments across different things so one bad bet cannot sink you.
terms.example: Owning 50 different stocks instead of one.

terms.plain: how wildly prices swing
terms.meaning: How much and how fast a price moves up and down.
terms.example: A stock that jumps 10% one day and drops 8% the next.

terms.plain: a period of rising prices
terms.meaning: A stretch when stock or asset prices keep going up and investors are optimistic.
terms.example: Stocks climbing steadily for years.

terms.plain: a period of falling prices
terms.meaning: A stretch when prices drop 20% or more from their high and investors are gloomy.
terms.example: Stocks sliding for months in 2008.

terms.plain: a modest price drop after a run-up
terms.meaning: A fall of roughly 10% from a recent high, less severe than a bear market.
terms.example: Stocks slipping 10% after a big rally.

terms.plain: a sudden, steep price collapse
terms.meaning: A very fast, very large drop in prices.
terms.example: Stocks losing 20% in a single day in 1987.

terms.plain: a quick rise in prices
terms.meaning: A period of rapidly rising prices.
terms.example: Stocks jumping 5% in a week after good news.

terms.plain: protection against a loss
terms.meaning: An investment made to offset the risk of another one.
terms.example: Buying insurance on your house.

terms.plain: a bet whose value depends on something else
terms.meaning: A financial contract whose value comes from an underlying asset like a stock, a currency, or oil.
terms.example: A contract that pays out if oil goes above $90 a barrel.
terms.plural: bets whose value depends on something else

terms.plain: tradeable financial products
terms.meaning: Things like stocks and bonds that can be bought and sold.
terms.example: Anything you might see in a brokerage account.

terms.plain: bundles of home loans sold to investors
terms.meaning: Home loans packaged together and sold as an investment. Investors get the monthly payments.
terms.example: Thousands of mortgages bundled into one product, famous from 2008.

terms.plain: bundling loans to sell as investments
terms.meaning: Turning a pool of loans into tradeable securities.
terms.example: A bank packaging 5,000 car loans and selling them to investors.

terms.plain: a grade for how safe a borrower is
terms.meaning: A score showing how likely a borrower is to pay back its debts.
terms.example: AAA is very safe; junk means risky.
terms.plural: grades for how safe borrowers are

terms.plain: extra return for taking extra risk
terms.meaning: The additional return investors demand for holding something riskier than a safe bet.
terms.example: A shaky company must pay 9% on its bonds while the government pays 4%.

terms.plain: profit from selling something for more than you paid
terms.meaning: The gain when you sell an asset at a higher price than you bought it.
terms.example: Buying shares at $50 and selling at $80.

terms.plain: what you got back compared to what you put in
terms.meaning: The profit from an investment as a percentage of its cost.
terms.example: Invest $100, end up with $110: a 10% return.

terms.plain: interest earning interest
terms.meaning: When the interest you earn is added to your balance, so the next round of interest is bigger.

terms.plain: the original amount borrowed or invested
terms.meaning: The base sum of a loan or investment, not counting interest.
terms.example: On a $200k mortgage, $200k is the principal.

terms.plain: paying off a loan bit by bit
terms.meaning: Spreading loan repayment over regular installments that cover both interest and the amount borrowed.
terms.example: A 30-year mortgage paid in 360 monthly chunks.

terms.plain: something you pledge to lose if you do not repay
terms.meaning: An asset the lender can take if you fail to pay back a loan.
terms.example: Your house on a mortgage, your car on a car loan.

terms.plain: what you own minus what you owe
terms.meaning: Total assets minus total debts.
terms.example: A $300k house and $50k savings minus a $200k mortgage is $150k net worth.

terms.plain: money coming in versus going out
terms.meaning: The movement of money into and out of a business or household over time.
terms.example: A shop taking in $10k a month and paying out $8k has positive cash flow.

terms.plain: total money taken in
terms.meaning: All the money a business receives from sales before any costs are subtracted.
terms.example: A lemonade stand selling 100 cups at $1 has $100 revenue.

terms.plain: money left after costs
terms.meaning: What is left from revenue after paying all expenses.
terms.example: $100 in lemonade sales minus $30 for lemons and sugar is $70 profit.

terms.plain: ongoing costs of running a business
terms.meaning: Costs that must be paid regardless of how much is sold.
terms.example: Rent, insurance, and electricity for a store.

terms.plain: costs that rise as you make more
terms.meaning: Expenses that go up with each extra unit produced.
terms.example: Flour and eggs for each extra cake.

terms.plain: the cost of things wearing out
terms.meaning: Spreading the cost of a machine or building over the years it is used.
terms.example: A $10k van written off at $2k a year for five years.

terms.plain: what a whole company is worth on the stock market
terms.meaning: The total value of all a company's shares.
terms.example: 10 million shares at $50 each means a $500 million company.

terms.plain: a company selling shares to the public for the first time
terms.meaning: An initial public offering: the first time a company's shares are sold on a stock exchange.
terms.example: A startup listing on the Nasdaq.

terms.plain: money invested in risky young companies
terms.meaning: Funding given to startups in exchange for ownership, in hope of a big payoff.
terms.example: A fund putting $5M into an app in exchange for 20% of it.

terms.plain: investors buying whole companies
terms.meaning: Funds that buy companies outright, often with borrowed money, to improve and resell them.
terms.example: A fund buying a chain of dental clinics.

terms.plain: a lightly regulated investment fund for the wealthy
terms.meaning: An investment pool that uses aggressive strategies and is open only to rich or institutional investors.
terms.example: A fund betting that a company's stock will fall.

terms.plain: a fund that simply owns the whole market
terms.meaning: A low-cost fund that holds every stock in an index like the S&P 500 rather than picking winners.
terms.example: One purchase that gives you a sliver of 500 big companies.

terms.plain: the 500 biggest US companies' stock index
terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 large US companies, used as shorthand for 'the stock market'.
terms.example: When the news says 'stocks rose', it usually means this.

terms.plain: hundredths of a percent
terms.meaning: One basis point is 0.01 percentage points. 100 basis points equals 1 percentage point.
terms.example: A rate going from 5.00% to 5.25% rose 25 basis points.

terms.plain: a home loan
terms.meaning: A loan used to buy a house, with the house as security.
terms.example: Borrowing $300k to buy a home and paying it back over 30 years.

terms.plain: the bank taking your house for missed payments
terms.meaning: When a lender seizes a home because the owner stopped paying the mortgage.
terms.example: A family losing their house after a year of missed payments.

terms.plain: owing more on your home than it is worth
terms.meaning: When your mortgage balance is bigger than your home's market value.
terms.example: Owing $300k on a house now worth $250k.

terms.plain: what families owe
terms.meaning: All the debt held by households: mortgages, car loans, credit cards, student loans.
terms.example: A family's combined mortgage, car payment, and credit card balance.

terms.plain: the share of income people save
terms.meaning: The percentage of take-home pay that households put away instead of spending.
terms.example: Earning $4,000 a month and saving $400 is a 10% savings rate.

terms.plain: how optimistic people feel about money
terms.meaning: A survey measure of how people feel about the economy and their own finances, which predicts spending.
terms.example: People planning vacations and big purchases when they feel secure.

terms.plain: spending more because you feel richer
terms.meaning: When rising home or stock values make people spend more, even if their income has not changed.
terms.example: Buying a boat because your house 'went up' $100k on paper.

terms.plain: the gap between what the rich and poor own
terms.meaning: How unevenly wealth is spread across a population.
terms.example: The top 1% owning a third of everything.

terms.plain: a 0-to-1 score for inequality
terms.meaning: A number measuring how unequal incomes are: 0 means everyone earns the same, 1 means one person has everything.
terms.example: A score of 0.25 is fairly equal; 0.50 is very unequal.

terms.plain: the income level below which you count as poor
terms.meaning: The minimum income the government says a household needs to cover basics.
terms.example: About $31,000 for a family of four in the US.

terms.plain: the middle income
terms.meaning: The income level where half of people earn more and half earn less. Less skewed by billionaires than the average.
terms.example: If five people earn $20k, $30k, $40k, $50k, and $5M, the median is $40k.

terms.plain: how comfortably people live
terms.meaning: The level of wealth, comfort, and goods available to people.
terms.example: Whether a typical family can afford a car, healthcare, and a vacation.

terms.plain: a regular cash payment to everyone
terms.meaning: A policy of giving every citizen a set amount of money regularly, no strings attached.
terms.example: Every adult receiving $1,000 a month from the government.

terms.plain: favoring government spending to steady the economy
terms.meaning: An approach, from economist John Maynard Keynes, that says governments should spend more in slumps to keep demand up.
terms.example: Building roads during a recession to keep people employed.

terms.plain: focusing on the money supply to control prices
terms.meaning: The view that inflation mainly comes from how much money is in circulation, so controlling the money supply is key.
terms.example: Milton Friedman's line: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

terms.plain: boosting the economy by cutting taxes and rules
terms.meaning: The idea that lower taxes and fewer regulations encourage businesses to produce more, which grows the economy.
terms.example: Cutting corporate taxes so companies invest more.

terms.plain: a school that distrusts central planning and central banks
terms.meaning: A school of thought that emphasizes free markets and sees government and central-bank meddling as the source of booms and busts.
terms.example: Blaming low interest rates for a housing bubble.

terms.plain: free markets, free trade, and a smaller government
terms.meaning: A broad label for policies favoring open markets, privatization, and less government involvement in the economy.
terms.example: Selling off state industries and cutting trade barriers in the 1980s and 90s.

terms.plain: the study of the whole economy
terms.meaning: The big-picture branch of economics: growth, inflation, unemployment, and government policy.
terms.example: Asking why the whole country is in a recession.

terms.plain: the study of individual choices and markets
terms.meaning: The small-picture branch: how people, households, and businesses make decisions and how single markets work.
terms.example: Asking why coffee costs $5 at this cafe.

terms.plain: all else being equal
terms.meaning: A Latin phrase meaning 'holding everything else the same', used to isolate one cause.
terms.example: If the price of apples rises, ceteris paribus, people buy fewer apples.

terms.plain: the trade-off between joblessness and rising prices
terms.meaning: The observation that when unemployment is low, inflation tends to be high, and vice versa.
terms.example: A hot job market pushing wages, and then prices, up.

terms.plain: the lowest unemployment can go without pushing prices up
terms.meaning: The level of unemployment that exists even in a healthy economy, from people moving between jobs.
terms.example: Around 4% in the US.

terms.plain: knock-on effect
terms.meaning: When new spending gets re-spent again and again, boosting the economy by more than the original amount.
terms.example: A $1,000 stimulus check pays a plumber, who pays a grocer, who pays a farmer.

terms.plain: how fast money changes hands
terms.meaning: How many times a dollar is spent in a year.
terms.example: The same $20 bill paying for lunch, then a haircut, then groceries in one week.

terms.plain: situation where cheap money stops working
terms.meaning: A situation where interest rates are near zero but people still will not borrow or spend, so cuts have no effect.
terms.example: Japan in the 1990s: free money, no takers.

terms.plain: interest rates cannot go below zero
terms.meaning: The problem that a central bank cannot cut rates much below zero, limiting its options in a deep slump.
terms.example: Rates at 0% with nowhere left to cut.

terms.plain: aiming for a set rate of price increases
terms.meaning: A central bank publicly aiming for a specific inflation rate, usually 2%.
terms.example: The Fed trying to keep prices rising about 2% a year.

terms.plain: the central bank hinting at its future moves
terms.meaning: A central bank telling the public what it plans to do with interest rates so people can plan.
terms.example: The Fed saying it expects to hold rates steady through next year.

terms.plain: what people think prices will do
terms.meaning: How much people expect prices to rise, which shapes their wage demands and spending.
terms.example: Workers asking for bigger raises because they expect prices to jump.

terms.plain: wages and prices chasing each other upward
terms.meaning: When rising prices lead to higher wage demands, which raise costs and prices further.
terms.example: Workers get 8% raises, shops raise prices 8%, workers ask for another raise.

terms.plain: prices rising because people want to buy more than is available
terms.meaning: Inflation caused by too much spending chasing too few goods.
terms.example: Everyone gets a bonus and rushes to buy the same limited stock of cars.

terms.plain: prices rising because making things got more expensive
terms.meaning: Inflation caused by higher costs, like wages or raw materials, being passed on to customers.
terms.example: Oil prices spike, so shipping and then groceries cost more.

terms.plain: new industries wiping out old ones
terms.meaning: The process where innovation destroys old businesses but creates better ones.
terms.example: Streaming killing video rental stores.

terms.plain: a gentle push toward a better choice
terms.meaning: Designing choices so people are steered toward a good option without forcing them.
terms.example: Making retirement saving the default so people have to opt out.

terms.plain: money already spent that you cannot get back
terms.meaning: A past cost that should not affect a decision, because it is gone either way.
terms.example: Finishing a bad movie because you paid for the ticket.

terms.plain: the study of strategic decisions
terms.meaning: The study of how people make choices when the outcome depends on what others do.
terms.example: Deciding whether to cut prices knowing your rival might too.

terms.plain: a situation where selfish choices leave everyone worse off
terms.meaning: A classic game where two people each do better by betraying the other, yet both lose if both betray.
terms.example: Two rival stores both slashing prices and both losing money.

terms.plain: no one can be made better off without hurting someone else
terms.meaning: A situation where resources are allocated so that improving one person's lot means worsening another's.
terms.example: A pie fully divided: giving anyone more means taking from someone.

terms.plain: value lost when a market is distorted
terms.meaning: The benefit that disappears when a tax, price control, or monopoly stops trades that would have helped both sides.
terms.example: A tax so high that some people stop buying and the seller stops selling, so no one gets that value.

terms.plain: the deal you got below what you would have paid
terms.meaning: The gap between what you were willing to pay and what you actually paid.
terms.example: Willing to pay $50 for a jacket, finding it for $30: $20 of surplus.

terms.plain: the extra a seller gets above their minimum price
terms.meaning: The gap between the lowest price a seller would accept and the price they actually got.
terms.example: Willing to sell for $20, selling for $30: $10 of surplus.

terms.plain: a measurement that signals how the economy is doing
terms.meaning: Any statistic used to judge the health of the economy.
terms.example: Unemployment, inflation, and GDP growth.
terms.plural: measurements that signal how the economy is doing

terms.plain: things slowing the economy down
terms.meaning: Obstacles that make growth harder.
terms.example: High interest rates and expensive fuel.

terms.plain: things helping the economy along
terms.meaning: Favorable conditions that make growth easier.
terms.example: Cheap energy and strong consumer spending.

terms.plain: the economy growing too fast to be healthy
terms.meaning: When demand is so strong that prices start rising too quickly.
terms.example: A job market so hot that employers cannot find workers and keep raising wages.

terms.plain: a sudden unexpected event that hits the economy
terms.meaning: An unforeseen jolt, like a war or pandemic, that disrupts normal activity.
terms.example: Oil prices doubling overnight after a conflict.
terms.plural: sudden unexpected events that hit the economy

terms.plain: a choke point slowing everything down
terms.meaning: One stage in a process that cannot keep up, holding up everything behind it.
terms.example: A single clogged port delaying goods across the country.

terms.plain: rate-cut-leaning
terms.meaning: Describes a central banker who favors keeping rates low to support jobs, even if prices rise a bit.
terms.example: A Fed official saying growth matters more than inflation right now.

terms.plain: rate-hike-leaning
terms.meaning: Describes a central banker who favors raising rates to fight inflation, even if it slows growth.
terms.example: A Fed official pushing for another rate hike.

terms.plain: making borrowing harder or costlier
terms.meaning: Raising interest rates or reducing the money supply to slow the economy.
terms.example: The Fed raising rates three times in a year.

terms.plain: making borrowing easier or cheaper
terms.meaning: Cutting interest rates or adding money to speed up the economy.
terms.example: The Fed cutting rates to help a weak job market.

terms.plain: an economy stuck with no growth
terms.meaning: A long stretch with little or no economic growth.
terms.example: Years of the economy barely budging.

terms.plain: a period of very fast growth
terms.meaning: A time of rapid expansion, high spending, and low unemployment.
terms.example: The late 1990s tech boom.

terms.plain: a sharp collapse after a boom
terms.meaning: A sudden downturn that follows a boom.
terms.example: The dot-com bust of 2000.

terms.plain: anyone affected by a decision
terms.meaning: A person or group with an interest in how something turns out.
terms.example: A company's workers, customers, and neighbors, not just its owners.

terms.plain: someone who owns part of a company
terms.meaning: A person or fund that owns shares in a company.
terms.example: Anyone with Apple stock in their retirement account.
terms.plural: people who own part of a company

terms.plain: turn into money
terms.meaning: To find a way to make money from something.
terms.example: A YouTuber running ads on their videos.

terms.plain: spending on big long-term items
terms.meaning: Money a business spends on buildings, equipment, and other things it will use for years.
terms.example: A trucking company buying ten new trucks.

terms.plain: day-to-day running costs
terms.meaning: The regular costs of keeping a business going.
terms.example: Salaries, rent, and utilities.

terms.plain: the share of sales left after making the product
terms.meaning: Revenue minus the direct cost of making what was sold, as a percentage of revenue.
terms.example: Sell a shirt for $20 that cost $8 to make: 60% gross margin.

terms.plain: two companies combining into one
terms.meaning: When two businesses join together.
terms.example: Two regional banks becoming one.

terms.plain: digital money not run by any government
terms.meaning: Money that exists only online and is tracked by a shared ledger rather than a bank.
terms.example: Bitcoin or Ethereum.

terms.plain: money that is valuable because the government says so
terms.meaning: Currency with no gold or other backing, whose value rests on trust in the government issuing it.
terms.example: The US dollar since 1971.

terms.plain: money backed by gold
terms.meaning: A system where currency can be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold.
terms.example: Trading a $20 bill for an ounce of gold at the bank, as in the 1800s.

terms.plain: short-term freelance work through apps
terms.meaning: An economy where many people work temporary jobs, often via apps, rather than as employees.
terms.example: Driving for Uber or delivering for DoorDash.

terms.plain: reusing and recycling instead of throwing away
terms.meaning: An economic model that keeps materials in use rather than making, using, and discarding.
terms.example: A company taking back old phones to recover the metals.

terms.plain: illegal buying and selling
terms.meaning: Trade that happens outside the law, often to avoid taxes or bans.
terms.example: Selling cigarettes without paying tax.

terms.plain: money migrants send home
terms.meaning: Money that workers abroad send back to family in their home country.
terms.example: A nurse in London wiring money to her parents in Manila.

terms.plain: skilled people leaving a country
terms.meaning: When educated workers emigrate, taking their skills elsewhere.
terms.example: Doctors trained in one country moving abroad for better pay.

terms.plain: smoothed to remove predictable seasonal swings
terms.meaning: A statistic corrected for regular yearly patterns, like holiday hiring, so months can be compared fairly.
terms.example: Retail sales look flat once the December shopping bump is stripped out.

terms.plain: scaled up to a full-year rate
terms.meaning: A short-period number stretched out to show what it would be over a whole year.
terms.example: Growth of 0.5% in one quarter is about 2% annualized.

terms.plain: compared to the same time last year
terms.meaning: A change measured against the same month or quarter a year earlier.
terms.example: Prices in March versus prices last March.

terms.plain: compared to the previous three months
terms.meaning: A change measured against the previous quarter.
terms.example: Sales this spring versus this winter.

terms.plain: a three-month period
terms.meaning: One quarter of a year, the standard unit for reporting economic and business results.
terms.example: January through March is the first quarter.

terms.plain: a company's or government's 12-month accounting year
terms.meaning: A 12-month period used for budgeting, which may not match the calendar year.
terms.example: The US government's year runs October through September.

terms.plain: a difference of one whole percent
terms.meaning: The simple difference between two percentages, as opposed to a percentage change.
terms.example: Going from 2% to 3% is a rise of 1 percentage point, but a 50% increase.

terms.plain: economics
terms.meaning: The study of how people, businesses, and countries decide what to do with limited time, money, and stuff.
terms.example: Why a student picks a job over a nap, or why a country builds roads instead of tanks.

terms.plain: a give-and-take choice
terms.meaning: Getting more of one thing means getting less of something else.
terms.example: An extra hour at work is an hour less with friends.

terms.plain: nothing is truly free
terms.meaning: Every choice costs something, even if no money changes hands, because you gave up the alternative.
terms.example: A 'free' concert still costs you the evening you could have spent elsewhere.
aliases: there is no such thing as a free lunch

terms.plain: getting the most out of what you have
terms.meaning: Squeezing the most value out of limited resources, with nothing wasted. The 'size of the pie'.
terms.example: A kitchen where every burner is in use and no food is thrown away.

terms.plain: wasting what you have
terms.meaning: Producing less than you could from your resources, or using them on the wrong things.
terms.example: A factory with half its machines idle.

terms.plain: how evenly wealth is shared
terms.meaning: How evenly the economy's benefits are spread across people. The 'slicing of the pie'.
terms.example: Two roommates splitting groceries 50/50 rather than one eating most of it.

terms.plain: people who weigh costs and benefits
terms.meaning: The textbook assumption that people do the best they can for themselves given their options, comparing what they gain against what they give up.
terms.example: Someone who checks whether the drive to a cheaper store is worth the gas.

terms.plain: a small extra step
terms.meaning: A small tweak to what you are already doing: one more, or one less.
terms.example: Deciding whether to study one more hour, not whether to study at all.

terms.plain: compare the next small step's costs and benefits
terms.meaning: Making decisions by asking whether one more unit is worth its extra cost, rather than all-or-nothing.
terms.example: An airline sells a last-minute seat for $50 because the extra passenger costs it almost nothing.

terms.plain: the extra benefit from one more
terms.meaning: What you gain from a small additional amount of something.
terms.example: The enjoyment from a third slice of pizza.

terms.plain: the extra cost of one more
terms.meaning: What it costs to produce or get one additional unit.
terms.example: The dough and cheese for one more pizza, not the oven.

terms.plain: an economy run by millions of buyers and sellers
terms.meaning: An economy where businesses and households decide what to make, buy, and sell, instead of a central government planner.
terms.example: Restaurants open where people want to eat, not where an official assigns them.

terms.plain: an economy run by government planners
terms.meaning: An economy where a central authority decides what gets made, how much, and who gets it.
terms.example: The Soviet Union deciding how many shoes each factory would produce.

terms.plain: a government official deciding what gets made
terms.meaning: Someone in government who decides what the economy should produce and who gets it, instead of leaving it to buyers and sellers.
terms.example: An official in Moscow in 1970 setting the number of tractors each factory must build.
terms.plural: government officials deciding what gets made

terms.plain: the legal right to own and control things
terms.meaning: The rules that let people own things and decide how they are used, backed by courts.
terms.example: A farmer will only plant if they know no one can legally take the harvest.

terms.plain: the ability to push prices around
terms.meaning: When a single buyer or seller is big enough to influence the market price instead of just accepting it.
terms.example: The only gas station for 50 miles charging what it likes.

terms.plain: test ideas against evidence
terms.meaning: Coming up with a theory, then checking it against real-world data.
terms.example: Guessing that higher prices cut sales, then looking at sales figures to see.

terms.plain: a simplified picture of how part of the economy works
terms.meaning: A diagram or equation that leaves out details to make one relationship easier to see.
terms.example: A subway map: not to scale, but it shows how to get around.
terms.plural: simplified pictures of how the economy works

terms.plain: a simplification taken as given
terms.meaning: Something assumed to be true to make a problem easier to think about.
terms.example: Pretending there are only two countries in the world to explain trade.

terms.plain: the money-goes-round map
terms.meaning: A simple picture showing money flowing from households to businesses when they buy things, and back to households as wages and profit.
terms.example: You pay a cafe for coffee; the cafe pays its barista, who buys coffee somewhere else.

terms.plain: the most-you-can-make curve
terms.meaning: A graph showing every combination of two things an economy could produce if it used everything it has. Points inside the curve are wasteful; points outside are impossible.
terms.example: A bakery with one oven can make 100 loaves, or 200 muffins, or some mix, but not both maxed out.

terms.plain: a claim about how things are
terms.meaning: A statement about facts that could in principle be checked against evidence.
terms.example: 'Raising the minimum wage reduces teen employment' is testable, whether or not it turns out true.

terms.plain: a claim about how things should be
terms.meaning: A statement of opinion or values that cannot be settled by evidence alone.
terms.example: 'The government should raise the minimum wage.'
terms.plural: claims about how things should be

terms.plain: being able to make more with the same resources
terms.meaning: Being flat-out better at producing something, using fewer inputs than someone else.
terms.example: A chef who can chop twice as many onions per hour as a trainee.

terms.plain: a market with many buyers and many sellers
terms.meaning: A market where there are so many buyers and sellers that no single one can affect the price.
terms.example: Wheat farmers: there are thousands, so no one farmer can raise the price.

terms.plain: someone who has to accept the going price
terms.meaning: A buyer or seller too small to influence the price, so they take it as given.
terms.example: A corn farmer selling at whatever the market pays that day.
terms.plural: people who have to accept the going price

terms.plain: the amount people will buy at a given price
terms.meaning: How much of something buyers are willing and able to buy at one specific price.
terms.example: At $2 a scoop, the town buys 500 ice creams a day.

terms.plain: the amount sellers will offer at a given price
terms.meaning: How much of something sellers are willing and able to sell at one specific price.
terms.example: At $2 a scoop, the shops are willing to sell 300 ice creams a day.

terms.plain: people buy less when the price goes up
terms.meaning: All else equal, a higher price means people buy less, and a lower price means they buy more.
terms.example: Sales of strawberries jump when they go on special.

terms.plain: sellers offer more when the price goes up
terms.meaning: All else equal, a higher price means sellers are willing to produce and sell more.
terms.example: More people pick up ride-share shifts when surge pricing is on.

terms.plain: prices settle where buying matches selling
terms.meaning: The price of anything moves to the level where the amount people want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.
terms.example: Concert tickets get pricier until exactly enough fans are willing to pay.
aliases: the law of supply and demand

terms.plain: a table of prices and how much people would buy
terms.meaning: A list showing, for each price, how much buyers would purchase.
terms.example: $1: 800 scoops, $2: 500 scoops, $3: 200 scoops.

terms.plain: the line showing how much people buy at each price
terms.meaning: A graph of the demand schedule. It slopes down because people buy less as the price rises.
terms.example: Plot price against ice creams bought and you get a downhill line.
terms.plural: lines showing how much people buy at each price

terms.plain: a table of prices and how much sellers would offer
terms.meaning: A list showing, for each price, how much sellers would sell.
terms.example: $1: 100 scoops, $2: 300 scoops, $3: 600 scoops.

terms.plain: the line showing how much sellers offer at each price
terms.meaning: A graph of the supply schedule. It slopes up because sellers offer more as the price rises.
terms.example: Plot price against ice creams offered and you get an uphill line.
terms.plural: lines showing how much sellers offer at each price

terms.plain: the amount bought and sold at the balance price
terms.meaning: How much changes hands when supply and demand are balanced.
terms.example: At $2, buyers want 400 and sellers offer 400, so 400 scoops are sold.

terms.plain: something you buy more of when you earn more
terms.meaning: A product people buy more of as their income rises.
terms.example: Restaurant meals, new clothes, vacations.
terms.plural: things you buy more of when you earn more

terms.plain: something you buy less of when you earn more
terms.meaning: A product people buy less of as their income rises, because they can now afford something better.
terms.example: Instant noodles and bus tickets, once you can afford steak and a car.
terms.plural: things you buy less of when you earn more

terms.plain: things you could buy instead of each other
terms.meaning: Two products where a price rise in one makes people buy more of the other.
terms.example: Coke and Pepsi, butter and margarine, movie tickets and streaming.

terms.plain: things you buy together
terms.meaning: Two products where a price rise in one makes people buy less of the other, because they go together.
terms.example: Hot dogs and buns, printers and ink, cars and gas.

terms.plain: things you swap one-for-one without caring
terms.meaning: Two products a buyer treats as completely interchangeable.
terms.example: A $10 bill and two $5 bills.

terms.plain: things only useful together in fixed amounts
terms.meaning: Two products that must be used together in a set ratio.
terms.example: Left shoes and right shoes.

terms.plain: how much sellers change output when the price changes
terms.meaning: A measure of how strongly the amount sellers offer responds to a price change.
terms.example: Beachfront land: the price doubles but there is no more of it to sell.

terms.plain: how much buying changes when income changes
terms.meaning: A measure of how strongly purchases respond to a change in people's income.
terms.example: A 10% raise and you eat out 20% more: eating out is very income-sensitive.

terms.plain: how much buying of one thing changes when another's price changes
terms.meaning: A measure of how the purchases of one product respond to a price change in a different product.
terms.example: Coffee gets pricier, so tea sales rise.

terms.plain: who really ends up paying a tax
terms.meaning: The question of who bears the cost of a tax, which is often not the person who hands the money over.
terms.example: A tax on landlords ends up in higher rents, so tenants pay part of it.

terms.plain: the study of how well off policies leave people
terms.meaning: The branch of economics that asks whether an arrangement makes people better or worse off overall.
terms.example: Working out whether a new bridge is worth its cost to everyone affected.

terms.plain: the most someone would pay
terms.meaning: The top price a buyer would hand over for something.
terms.example: You'd pay up to $40 for the concert, so at $25 you feel like you got a deal.

terms.plain: making people feel the side effects of their actions
terms.meaning: Changing incentives so that people take into account the costs or benefits they impose on others.
terms.example: A carbon tax makes a polluter pay for the harm it causes.

terms.plain: a tax that makes polluters pay for the harm they cause
terms.meaning: A tax designed to make a business or person face the cost they impose on others.
terms.example: A tax on cigarettes or carbon emissions.
terms.plural: taxes that make polluters pay for the harm they cause

terms.plain: people can fix side effects by bargaining if bargaining is cheap
terms.meaning: The idea that if the people involved can negotiate easily, they will sort out an externality themselves without government help.
terms.example: A neighbor pays the other to keep the dog quiet, or vice versa, whoever values it more.

terms.plain: the hassle and expense of making a deal
terms.meaning: The time, money, and effort it takes to reach and enforce an agreement.
terms.example: Lawyer fees, haggling, and paperwork when selling a house.

terms.plain: being able to stop people who don't pay
terms.meaning: Whether a seller can keep non-payers from using something.
terms.example: A cinema can stop you at the door; a fireworks show cannot.

terms.plain: one person's use leaves less for others
terms.meaning: Whether one person using something reduces what is left for everyone else.
terms.example: A slice of pizza is rival; a radio broadcast is not.

terms.plain: things you can be charged for and that get used up
terms.meaning: Goods that a seller can withhold from non-payers and that one person's use leaves less for others. Most things in shops.
terms.example: A sandwich.

terms.plain: things you can be charged for but that don't run out
terms.meaning: Goods that non-payers can be excluded from, but that many people can use at once without using them up.
terms.example: Netflix or a private golf course.

terms.plain: shared things anyone can use but that run out
terms.meaning: Goods that nobody can be stopped from using, but that get depleted as people use them.
terms.example: Fish in the ocean, a public parking lot.

terms.plain: someone who benefits without paying
terms.meaning: A person who enjoys something others paid for while contributing nothing.
terms.example: Watching the town fireworks without chipping in.

terms.plain: weighing what something costs against what it's worth
terms.meaning: Adding up all the costs and all the benefits of a project to see if it is worth doing.
terms.example: Is a $2 million bridge worth it if it saves each commuter 20 minutes a day?

terms.plain: the share of your total income paid in tax
terms.meaning: Total taxes divided by total income.
terms.example: Earn $50k, pay $8k tax: a 16% average rate.

terms.plain: a tax that is the same amount for everyone
terms.meaning: A fixed tax that does not change with income or spending.
terms.example: Every adult pays $1,000, whether they earn $20k or $2M.

terms.plain: you pay for what you use
terms.meaning: The idea that taxes should be based on how much a person benefits from government services.
terms.example: Gas taxes paying for roads: drivers pay, drivers benefit.

terms.plain: those who can afford more should pay more
terms.meaning: The idea that taxes should be based on how easily a person can bear them.
terms.example: A millionaire paying a higher share than a cashier.

terms.plain: richer people paying more
terms.meaning: The idea that people with more ability to pay should pay more tax.
terms.example: A higher tax bracket for higher earners.

terms.plain: similar people paying similar tax
terms.meaning: The idea that people in the same financial position should pay the same tax.
terms.example: Two families earning $60k paying the same, regardless of how they earned it.

terms.plain: a flat-rate tax
terms.meaning: A tax that takes the same percentage from everyone regardless of income.
terms.example: Everyone pays 15%, whether they earn $30k or $300k.

terms.plain: all the money a business takes in
terms.meaning: Price times quantity sold, before any costs are subtracted.
terms.example: 100 lemonades at $2 each: $200.

terms.plain: everything a business spends to produce
terms.meaning: The full amount a business pays for all its inputs.
terms.example: Lemons, sugar, cups, and the stand: $60.

terms.plain: costs paid out in cash
terms.meaning: Expenses that involve actually handing over money.
terms.example: Rent, wages, ingredients.

terms.plain: costs of what you gave up, with no cash paid
terms.meaning: Costs that do not involve a payment, like the salary you could have earned elsewhere.
terms.example: Quitting a $60k job to open a cafe costs you $60k a year, even though you never write a check.

terms.plain: revenue minus cash expenses
terms.meaning: What is left after subtracting only the costs actually paid out.
terms.example: Cafe takes in $150k and pays $100k in bills: $50k accounting profit.

terms.plain: revenue minus all costs, including what you gave up
terms.meaning: Profit after subtracting both the bills paid and the value of the alternatives you sacrificed.
terms.example: That $50k accounting profit is really a $10k loss if you gave up a $60k job for it.

terms.plain: how much output you get from a given amount of input
terms.meaning: The relationship between the inputs a business uses and how much it produces.
terms.example: One baker makes 50 loaves, two make 90, three make 120.

terms.plain: the extra output from one more unit of input
terms.meaning: How much more gets produced when one more worker or machine is added.
terms.example: Adding a second baker raises output from 50 to 90 loaves, so their marginal product is 40.

terms.plain: the extra output from one more worker
terms.meaning: How much more a business produces when it hires one additional worker.
terms.example: The third baker adds 30 loaves a day.

terms.plain: each extra worker adds less than the last
