terms.meaning: The pattern where adding more of one input, with everything else fixed, yields smaller and smaller gains.
terms.example: The tenth cook in a tiny kitchen mostly gets in the way.

terms.plain: costs you pay no matter how much you make
terms.meaning: Expenses that stay the same regardless of output.
terms.example: Rent on the shop is due whether you sell 10 pies or 1,000.

terms.plain: the cost per unit
terms.meaning: Total cost divided by the number of units made.
terms.example: $1,000 of costs for 500 pies: $2 per pie.

terms.plain: the fixed cost spread per unit
terms.meaning: Fixed costs divided by the number of units made. It falls as you make more.
terms.example: $500 rent over 500 pies is $1 each; over 1,000 pies it is 50 cents.

terms.plain: the variable cost per unit
terms.meaning: Variable costs divided by the number of units made.
terms.example: $500 of ingredients for 500 pies: $1 per pie.

terms.plain: the money taken in per unit
terms.meaning: Total revenue divided by the number of units sold. For most sellers it equals the price.
terms.example: $1,000 from 500 pies: $2 each.

terms.plain: the output level with the lowest cost per unit
terms.meaning: The amount of production at which the cost per unit is as low as it gets.
terms.example: The bakery is cheapest per loaf when it bakes about 800 a day.

terms.plain: cost per unit stays the same as you grow
terms.meaning: When doubling all inputs doubles output, so the cost per unit does not change.
terms.example: Two identical food trucks cost twice as much and make twice the tacos.

terms.plain: getting more expensive per unit as you grow
terms.meaning: When a business gets so large that each extra unit costs more, usually because it becomes hard to manage.
terms.example: A chain so big that head office cannot keep track of its stores.

terms.plain: a market where one big supplier is cheapest
terms.meaning: A situation where one company can serve the whole market more cheaply than two or more could, usually because of huge setup costs.
terms.example: Water pipes: it makes no sense to lay two sets of pipes down every street.

terms.plain: charging different people different prices for the same thing
terms.meaning: Selling the same product at different prices to different customers based on what they are willing to pay.
terms.example: Student discounts, senior fares, and cheaper matinee tickets.

terms.plain: many sellers with slightly different products
terms.meaning: A market with many competitors whose products are similar but not identical, so each has a little pricing power.
terms.example: Restaurants, hair salons, coffee shops.

terms.plain: a standoff where no one gains by changing alone
terms.meaning: A situation where each person is doing the best they can given what everyone else is doing, so nobody wants to change.
terms.example: Two gas stations across the street both charging $3.50: neither gains by moving first.

terms.plain: the best move no matter what others do
terms.meaning: A choice that works out best for you regardless of what the other players choose.
terms.example: Confessing in the prisoners' dilemma is best whether or not your partner confesses.

terms.plain: what one more worker's output is worth
terms.meaning: The extra output from one more worker, multiplied by the price it sells for. It tells a business the most it should pay that worker.
terms.example: A barista who brings in $25 an hour of extra coffee sales is worth up to $25 an hour.

terms.plain: extra pay for an unpleasant or risky job
terms.meaning: A wage difference that makes up for a job being dirtier, more dangerous, or less pleasant.
terms.example: Night-shift workers and offshore oil riggers earning more for the same skill level.

terms.plain: paying above the going rate to get better work
terms.meaning: Wages deliberately set higher than necessary so workers try harder and stay longer.
terms.example: Henry Ford doubling wages to $5 a day to cut turnover.

terms.plain: doing something visible to prove your quality
terms.meaning: Taking an action, like getting a degree, mainly to show others something they cannot see directly.
terms.example: A college diploma telling employers you can finish hard things.

terms.plain: testing people to sort out the good ones
terms.meaning: Actions an uninformed party takes to learn what the other side knows.
terms.example: An insurer requiring a medical exam before selling life insurance.

terms.plain: discrimination
terms.meaning: In economics, paying or treating people differently based on race, sex, age, or similar traits rather than their productivity.
terms.example: Two equally skilled applicants, one offered less because of their gender.

terms.plain: judging a person by their group's average
terms.meaning: Treating an individual based on averages about their group, rather than facts about them.
terms.example: Charging young drivers more for insurance because young drivers crash more on average.

terms.plain: union
terms.meaning: A group of workers who bargain together with their employer over pay and conditions.
terms.example: Teachers negotiating a contract as one block instead of one by one.

terms.plain: strike
terms.meaning: Workers refusing to work, as a group, to pressure the employer into a better deal.
terms.example: Auto workers walking out until they get a raise.

terms.plain: help given as goods or services instead of cash
terms.meaning: Government aid that comes as actual stuff, not money.
terms.example: Food stamps, housing vouchers, free school lunches.

terms.plain: the government paying money to low earners
terms.meaning: A system where people below a certain income receive a payment instead of paying tax.
terms.example: Earn $10k and get a $3k check from the government.

terms.plain: government programs that protect against bad luck
terms.meaning: Programs everyone pays into that pay out when someone is hit by unemployment, illness, or old age.
terms.example: Unemployment benefits and Social Security.

terms.plain: your normal long-run income
terms.meaning: What a person expects to earn on average over their life, ignoring temporary ups and downs.
terms.example: A commission salesperson who spends based on their typical year, not a bumper month.

terms.plain: the pattern of earning and spending over a lifetime
terms.meaning: The regular pattern of low income when young, high income mid-career, and low income in retirement.
terms.example: Borrowing as a student, saving in your forties, spending savings at seventy.

terms.plain: aim for the greatest total happiness
terms.meaning: The view that policy should maximize the total well-being of everyone in society added together.
terms.example: Taking $1 from a millionaire to give a hungry person a meal, because it raises total happiness.

terms.plain: design society as if you didn't know who you'd be
terms.meaning: The view, from philosopher John Rawls, that fair rules are the ones you would choose without knowing whether you would end up rich or poor.
terms.example: Picking the rules of a game before you know which team you will play for.

terms.plain: make the worst-off person as well off as possible
terms.meaning: The idea that a society should judge itself by how its poorest member is doing.
terms.example: Judging a school by how its weakest student does, not its star pupil.

terms.plain: let people keep what they earn
terms.meaning: The view that the government should protect property rights and enforce contracts but not redistribute income.
terms.example: Arguing that taxing one person to help another is unjust however good the cause.

terms.plain: what you can afford
terms.meaning: The limit on the combinations of things a person can buy with their income.
terms.example: With $20 you can get four coffees, or two coffees and a sandwich, but not both maxed.

terms.plain: the line of combinations you like equally
terms.meaning: A curve showing all the mixes of two things that give a person the same satisfaction.
terms.example: Three pizzas and one movie feels just as good to you as one pizza and three movies.
terms.plural: lines of combinations you like equally

terms.plain: how much of one thing you'd trade for one more of another
terms.meaning: The rate at which a person is willing to swap one good for another while staying equally happy.
terms.example: Giving up two sodas for one extra slice of pizza.

terms.plain: buying more because you feel richer
terms.meaning: The change in what you buy that happens because a price change leaves you with more or less spending power.
terms.example: Gas gets cheaper, so you feel richer and eat out more.

terms.plain: switching to what got relatively cheaper
terms.meaning: The change in what you buy that happens because one thing is now a better deal compared to another.
terms.example: Beef gets pricier, so you buy chicken instead.

terms.plain: a rare thing people buy more of when its price rises
terms.meaning: An unusual product where a price increase actually raises the amount bought, because poor buyers can no longer afford anything else.
terms.example: Rice for a very poor family: pricier rice leaves no money for meat, so they eat even more rice.

terms.plain: disliking uncertainty
terms.meaning: Preferring a sure thing over a gamble with the same average payoff.
terms.example: Taking $50 for certain rather than a coin flip for $100 or nothing.

terms.plain: someone acting for you not fully sharing your goals
terms.meaning: The tension when one person (the agent) makes decisions on behalf of another (the principal) but has different interests.
terms.example: A real estate agent nudging you to accept a quick sale because their commission is nearly the same either way.

terms.plain: how politics shapes economic decisions
terms.meaning: The study of how governments actually make economic choices, given voters, politicians, and their incentives.
terms.example: Why a subsidy survives long after economists say it should go.

terms.plain: majority votes can go round in circles
terms.meaning: The finding that majority voting can rank A over B, B over C, and yet C over A, so there is no clear winner.
terms.example: Three friends voting on pizza, tacos, or sushi and never settling it.

terms.plain: no voting system is perfectly fair
terms.meaning: A proof that no method of combining people's rankings into a group ranking can satisfy every reasonable fairness rule at once.
terms.example: Every election system has some situation where it gives an odd result.

terms.plain: politicians chase the voter in the middle
terms.meaning: The idea that in a majority vote, the outcome ends up being what the middle-of-the-road voter wants.
terms.example: Both parties drifting toward the center before an election.

terms.plain: using statistics on economic data
terms.meaning: The toolkit economists use to test theories with real-world numbers.
terms.example: Estimating how much a 10% price cut boosts sales by crunching past sales data.

terms.plain: an experiment with a coin-flip control group
terms.meaning: A study where people are randomly assigned to get a treatment or not, so the two groups can be fairly compared.
terms.example: Randomly giving half the villages cash grants and comparing them to the other half.

terms.plain: numbers from a controlled experiment
terms.meaning: Data collected by deliberately changing one thing and watching what happens.
terms.example: Sales figures from stores where you randomly changed the price.

terms.plain: numbers from watching the real world
terms.meaning: Data collected by observing what happens naturally, without controlling anything.
terms.example: Past sales figures and past prices, just as they happened.

terms.plain: a real-world event that acts like an experiment
terms.meaning: A situation where something outside anyone's control splits people into groups that can be compared.
terms.example: Comparing two neighboring states after one raises its minimum wage.

terms.plain: a hidden factor that muddles the result
terms.meaning: Something left out of the analysis that affects both the cause and the effect you are studying, making them look linked.
terms.example: Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer; hot weather is the hidden factor.

terms.plain: the effect actually causing the cause
terms.meaning: Mistaking which way the influence runs between two things.
terms.example: Do police cause crime because high-crime cities have more police? No, crime causes more police.

terms.plain: a snapshot of many people at one time
terms.meaning: Data on many different people, firms, or places measured at a single point in time.
terms.example: The incomes of 1,000 households this year.

terms.plain: one thing tracked over time
terms.meaning: Data on a single person, firm, or place measured repeatedly over many periods.
terms.example: US unemployment every month since 1950.

terms.plain: many people tracked over time
terms.meaning: Data that follows the same group of people, firms, or places across several periods.
terms.example: The same 1,000 households surveyed every year for a decade.

terms.plain: fitting a straight line through the data
terms.meaning: A statistical method that finds the straight line best describing how one thing changes with another.
terms.example: Drawing the best line through a scatter of price and sales points to see how much sales drop per dollar.

terms.plain: fitting a line with several factors at once
terms.meaning: A regression that accounts for more than one influence at the same time.
terms.example: Estimating how price, advertising, and weather together affect sales.

terms.plain: the standard way to fit the line
terms.meaning: The usual method for fitting a regression: choose the line that keeps the total squared gaps to the data smallest.
terms.example: The line that comes closest to all the dots at once.

terms.plain: how uncertain an estimate is
terms.meaning: A measure of how much an estimated number would bounce around if you repeated the study with new data.
terms.example: An effect of 5 with a standard error of 1 is solid; with a standard error of 6 it could easily be zero.
